instructions: Put the 2/3 cup bulgur in a bowl and pour in enough boiling water to cover it by an inch. Cover the bowl and leave it for 20 minutes.
Peel the potatoes and cut them into big chunks. Put them in a pot, cover with cold water and stir in 1 tsp of the salt.
Bring the pot to a boil over high heat. Turn it down to medium and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until a knife slides into a chunk with no resistance.

Quarter the onion. Put it in a food processor with the thyme leaves, basil leaves, 7 spice, 1 1/2 tsp salt, the pepper and 1 tbsp of the olive oil. Pulse until it's a coarse, thick paste. No processor? Mince everything as fine as you can and mash it together with a fork.
Drain the potatoes and mash them until smooth. Spread the mash on a tray and leave it for about 10 minutes, until it's no longer warm.
Drain the bulgur in a sieve and press out the water.
In a large bowl, mix the cooled potato, the bulgur and the herb paste with your hands until there are no lumps and it holds together.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Spread the kibbeh about an inch thick on a platter and press a pattern into the top with the back of a spoon. Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp olive oil over it.
Serve it cold. Leftovers keep in a covered container in the fridge for 3 days.
method_notes: Plant Based Folk (5.0 from 33) and Zaatar and Zaytoun both make this as a cold, no-bake mashed potato and bulgur dish, so that's what is written. The list's line says it is baked in a tray, but that is not how the sources make kibbet batata; the baked version is a different dish (kibbeh bil sanieh, like the existing Baked Kibbeh). Amounts are the lead's, scaled from 6 servings to 4. Zaatar and Zaytoun adds walnuts, tomato and pomegranate molasses, which are left out to keep it nut-free and simple.
